source_user: An agent repeatedly calls a calculator when the answer is already known. Design metrics and an intervention. Scenario variant 1: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure unnecessary calls, tool success, final correctness, trajectory length, tool latency, and recovery; add a stop/no-tool evaluation and preference or reward signal.
corrected_answer: For variant 1, assume calculator availability, inputs, model/version, prompt policy, task mix, and correctness labels are stable and that a call is unnecessary only when the final answer can be produced correctly without external arithmetic. Instrument every request and trajectory with task ID, calculator-call count and reason, tool arguments/result/errors, time spent in tool and total wall time in milliseconds, token usage, final correctness, abstention, retries, and recovery outcome. Report unnecessary-call rate, tool success/error rate, correctness, trajectory length, p50/p95/p99 latency, cost, and recovery rate, stratified by task type and difficulty; retain traces with privacy controls. Falsifiable hypothesis: on a prespecified held-out task mix, a stop/no-tool gate will reduce unnecessary calculator calls by at least 30% and tool-adjusted p95 latency by at least 10% without lowering final correctness by more than 1 percentage point. Randomize comparable requests to current policy versus the gate, keep model, hardware, timeout, prompt, and traffic mix fixed, and use disjoint tuning and evaluation sets. Tune the gate threshold only on training data; use paired bootstrap confidence intervals and predefined non-inferiority and latency tests. Check confounders including task mix, answer difficulty, cache hits, queueing, tool failures, retries, prompt changes, and correlated traffic. Add a no-tool evaluation and a tool-needed evaluation so the intervention does not suppress necessary calculations; use preference/reward data penalizing needless calls while rewarding correct tool use and calibrated abstention. Roll back immediately on correctness/SLO, safety, or recovery regressions, elevated hallucinated arithmetic, or tool-call error spikes; canary and version the policy, with an owner and an audit trail. Results are provisional and require domain-expert review.
risks: A learned gate may suppress calculator use on tasks that only appear easy.
Correctness labels and the definition of unnecessary use may be noisy.
Traffic mix, caching, queueing, or tool outages can confound latency and call-rate changes.
evidence_required: Paired held-out A/B results with confidence intervals for call rate, correctness, latency, cost, and recovery.
Stratified no-tool versus tool-needed evaluation and trace audit.
Canary rollback evidence under representative load and failure injection.
